extracted.intended_audience: statesmen, policymakers, political theorists, and students of government
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic principles and normative criteria for designing and evaluating federal constitutions (division of powers, legislative structure, executive prerogatives, and institutional checks) with comparative illustrations. Focused on how to balance state and national authority and the practical consequences of institutional choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated federal powers; residuary to states
rubrics_metrics.description: “The attributes of the Federal Government were therefore carefully enumerated and all that was not included amongst them was declared to constitute a part of the privileges of the several Governments of the States.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal powers should be clearly defined and limited; matters not enumerated belong to the states. This preserves state rule and makes the confederal government the exception. (Example: where Congress has a right but neglects to legislate, States may act until Congress provides a general law.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate governments may legislate in gaps until federal action
rubrics_metrics.description: “Whenever the exclusive right of regulating certain matters is not reserved to Congress by the Constitution, the States may take up the affair until it is brought before the National Assembly. For instance, Congress has the right of making a general law on bankruptcy, which, however, it neglects to do. Each State is then at liberty to make a law for itself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: allow states to fill legislative voids when the national legislature has not exercised its enumerated power; courts have upheld this practice. This reduces paralysis from unexercised federal authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: High federal court to maintain balance of power
rubrics_metrics.description: “A high Federal court was created ... destined, amongst other functions, to maintain the balance of power which had been established by the Constitution between the two rival Governments.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create an independent national judiciary to resolve disputes over federal vs state competence rather than leaving such questions to ordinary state courts, preventing partisan local adjudication of federal limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive external prerogatives for the Union
rubrics_metrics.description: “The exclusive right of making peace and war, of concluding treaties of commerce, of raising armies, and equipping fleets, was granted to the Union.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrate foreign policy, war-making, treaty-making, and national defense in the central government to ensure a coherent external policy and single representative in international affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal control of national systems and infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Union was invested with the power of controlling the monetary system, of directing the post office, and of opening the great roads which were to establish a communication between the different parts of the country.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign to the central government matters that require uniformity and national coordination (currency, communications, major transport arteries, patents, bankruptcy) to promote economic integration and efficient administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on state powers to protect the Union
rubrics_metrics.description: “They were forbidden to enact ex post facto laws, or to create a class of nobles in their community.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impose specific prohibitions on subordinate governments where their actions would threaten fundamental rights or the character of the Union (e.g., retroactive criminal laws, creation of hereditary classes).

rubrics_metrics.name: National taxing power to fulfil federal engagements
rubrics_metrics.description: “It was endowed with an unlimited power of levying taxes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant the central government sufficient revenue-raising authority so it can meet its obligations; otherwise federal commitments will be unenforceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization through single legislature and tribunal
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is but one tribunal to interpret, as there is one legislature to make the laws; and an impost voted by the representatives of the nation is binding upon all the citizens.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single national legislature and court create uniform law and policy binding on all citizens, increasing central authority relative to fragmented systems with multiple sovereign courts or parliaments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bicameral compromise: balance state independence and national sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: “The principle of the independence of the States prevailed in the formation of the Senate, and that of the sovereignty of the nation predominated in the composition of the House of Representatives.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design a two-chamber legislature where one house reflects territorial/state equality and the other reflects popular proportionality as a compromise between competing principles; expect trade-offs and logical inconsistencies as a result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition rules: equal-state Senate vs population-based House
rubrics_metrics.description: “It was decided that each State should send two senators to Congress, and a number of representatives proportioned to its population.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use equal representation in one chamber to protect smaller polities and proportional representation in the other to reflect popular sovereignty. Be aware this can produce institutional tensions and potential paralysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional risk of Senate minority paralyzing House majority
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the minority of the nation preponderates in the Senate, it may paralyze the decisions of the majority represented in the other House, which is contrary to the spirit of constitutional government.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the anti-majoritarian risk inherent in a bicameral arrangement where a chamber representing states equally can block the popular will; mitigate through procedural design or political norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different election methods, terms, and functions for the two houses
rubrics_metrics.description: “The House of Representatives is named by the people, the Senate by the legislators of each State ... the term for which the representatives are chosen is only two years, that of the senators is six. The functions of the House of Representatives are purely legislative ... The Senate ... tries those political offences ... acts as the great executive council of the nation; the treaties which are concluded by the President must be ratified by the Senate, and the appointments he may make must be definitely approved by the same body.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate differing term lengths, selection methods (direct vs indirect), and institutional roles to chambers to embody different principles (responsiveness vs stability, popular will vs state interest, legislative vs advisory/judicial roles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive: elective, responsible, and partially independent
rubrics_metrics.description: “The President is an elective magistrate. ... He is free to act in his own sphere under the inspection, but not under the direction, of the Senate.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the executive to be accountable (elective) yet able to act independently within its sphere, subject to oversight but not subject to parliamentary direction. Balance independence and responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms to protect executive independence (fixed salary, suspensive veto)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The salary of the President is fixed, at the time of his entering upon office, for the whole period of his magistracy. The President is, moreover, provided with a suspensive veto ... forces [the legislature] at least to reconsider the matter ... it must then be backed by a majority of two-thirds of the whole house.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide institutional protections that prevent legislative co-optation (e.g., fixed compensation, suspensive veto requiring supermajorities to override) so the executive can plead its case to the people and resist short-term legislative encroachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid executive councils that dilute responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: “The President was made the sole representative of the executive power of the Union, and care was taken not to render his decisions subordinate to the vote of a council—a dangerous measure, which tends at the same time to clog the action of the Government and to diminish its responsibility.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrate executive authority in a single accountable office rather than a collegial council to preserve clear responsibility and avoid administrative gridlock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive powers should be limited if office is elective
rubrics_metrics.description: “The dangers of the system of election applied to the head of the executive government ... may be more or less formidable in proportion to the place which the executive power occupies ... To attempt to render the representative of the State a powerful sovereign, and at the same time elective, is, in my opinion, to entertain two incompatible designs.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the head of state is elected, circumscribe the scope of executive prerogatives; electing a powerful sovereign risks ambition, factionalism, and instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual factors determine real executive strength
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the existence of the Union were perpetually threatened, ... the executive government would assume an increased importance ... The President of the United States is the commander-in-chief of the army, but of an army composed of only six thousand men; he commands the fleet, but the fleet reckons but few sail; he conducts the foreign relations of the Union, but the United States are a nation without neighbors.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for geography, external threats, military capacity, and international circumstances: constitutional powers may be weak in peacetime/isolation but become potent under external pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenure/durability increases executive power
rubrics_metrics.description: “The authority of the King, in France, has, in the first place, the advantage of duration over that of the President, and durability is one of the chief elements of strength; nothing is either loved or feared but what is likely to endure.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer terms or hereditary succession increase the staying power and practical influence of executives; shorter elective terms reduce permanence and thus practical authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elective system reduces administrative continuity around elections
rubrics_metrics.description: “In elective States, ... the wheels of government cease to act, as it were, of their own accord at the approach of an election ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect interruptions or slowdowns in governance around election cycles; consider institutional designs that preserve administrative continuity if continuous governance is desired.
